name: Bumble
tagline: Dating and connection app where, on the hetero side, women message first.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Bumble is freemium with multiple paid tiers and consumable boosts that vary by region and platform.

verdictSummary: The app itself is a swipe deck, a chat screen, and a filter query. Any competent agent can build that in an afternoon, and it will be completely useless, because the product is not the UI, it is the several million other people already inside it. A dating app with one user is a mirror. Add to that the moderation, photo verification, abuse reporting, and safety tooling that exist because strangers meeting strangers goes wrong in ways a personal project cannot absorb. Build the swipe deck if you want to learn; do not expect to date anyone through it.
coreLoopDIY: A local, passcode-gated matching app for a closed group you already know, plus a private tracker for who you are talking to and where it stands.
requirements: A real group of actual humans willing to join, which is the part no code solves
whatYouLose: The entire dating pool, which is the product
Photo verification, moderation, blocking, and reporting infrastructure
Mobile apps with push notifications people actually open
Matching and ranking tuned on years of behavioral data
Any plausible deniability when something goes wrong between two strangers
moatNotes: Two-sided liquidity with a hard local constraint: the pool has to be dense in your actual city, not globally.
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay Bumble for throughput, not features. The paid tiers mostly buy more attempts and more visibility in a pool that already has the people in it, and nobody is paying for a swipe animation. That is why a self-hosted clone does not compete: you can replicate every screen and still have zero inventory. The only honest DIY version is a closed-group matcher for a community that already exists offline, where you supply the liquidity yourself.
notes: The swipe deck is a one-sitting build; the other three million people are not. The moat is two-sided marketplace liquidity in your specific city, plus the safety and verification apparatus that makes strangers willing to show up.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted "closed circle matcher" for a group that already knows each other, plus a private dating pipeline tracker. Local only, no cloud, no signup emails.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Next.js 14 App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind. SQLite via better-sqlite3. Nothing else.
- Single shared passcode in .env (CIRCLE_PASSCODE) gates the whole app via middleware and an httpOnly cookie. No OAuth, no accounts provider, no email.
- Images: local uploads written to ./uploads, served through a route handler. Do not call any external storage.

In scope:
1. Profile: display name, age, a short bio, up to 3 photos, and 5 freeform tags. One profile per passcode-holder, keyed by a self-chosen handle stored in a cookie.
2. Deck: a card stack of every other profile in the circle, excluding ones already acted on. Buttons: pass, like. Keyboard arrows too.
3. Mutual match: when two handles like each other, create a match row and show it in a Matches list.
4. Chat: dead simple per-match message thread, polling every 3 seconds. No websockets, no typing indicators, no read receipts.
5. Pipeline tracker, separate from the circle: a private table only visible to the current handle. Columns: person, where you met, stage (talking, date scheduled, dated, faded, done), next step, last contact date, notes. Full CRUD, sortable by last contact, with a "gone quiet for 7+ days" highlight.
6. Seed script that inserts 6 fake profiles so the deck is not empty on first run.

Out of scope, do not build:
- Public signup, discovery of strangers, geolocation, distance filters, payments, boosts, push notifications, native apps, photo verification, moderation queues, or any recommendation model. Ranking is random with a stable seed.

Deliver: a README with setup, .env.example containing CIRCLE_PASSCODE, a migration script, the seed script, and an npm run dev that works in an empty folder after install. Keep the whole thing under roughly 900 lines and make the pipeline tracker the part that actually feels good to use, since that is the half of this you will keep.
